analysis.one_liner: Bans unlimited 'soft money' from national party committees and tightens federal campaign finance disclosure rules.
analysis.headline: The Campaign Reform Act of 1997 drew zero cosponsors and died in the Senate Rules Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have banned national political party committees from raising or spending unlimited, unregulated 'soft money' — the big contributions from corporations, unions, and wealthy donors that sat outside normal campaign finance limits. It would have closed routes for routing that money through tax-exempt groups, required faster public disclosure of large independent spending, increased fines for violations, banned using campaign funds for personal expenses, and stopped members of Congress from sending mass taxpayer-funded mail in their election years. As a trade-off, it doubled the individual contribution limit to candidates from $1,000 to $2,000. The bill never got a hearing, a vote, or even a cosponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary voters get more visibility into who is paying for political advertising and elections, and the role of six- and seven-figure checks to party committees is reduced. Candidates who rely on many small donors rather than big soft-money checks would face a more level field.

how_it_helps.text: National party committees and any entities they control would be barred from soliciting, receiving, or spending any money not subject to federal contribution limits and reporting rules, and state and local party committees would have to pay for any federal-election activity from federally regulated funds.
Party committees could no longer solicit funds for or donate to 501(c) tax-exempt organizations, closing a common channel for unreported political money.

Anyone spending $10,000 or more on election-related activity, and anyone making independent expenditures of $1,000 or more in the final weeks, would have to disclose it to the Federal Election Commission within 24 to 48 hours, and the bill defines 'express advocacy' to cover ads that a reasonable person would understand as supporting or opposing a candidate.

Campaign funds could no longer be converted to personal use — covering mortgages, clothing, vacations, country club dues, tuition, and entertainment tickets — and penalties for knowing and willful violations rise from the greater of $10,000 or 200% of the violation to $15,000 or 300%.
Members of Congress could not send franked (taxpayer-paid) mass mailings during an election year unless they had publicly announced they were not running.
Contributions from people not qualified to register to vote would be banned, and the FEC would gain authority to seek court injunctions and conduct random post-election audits.

analysis.who_pays: National party committees lose the unrestricted soft-money channel, and the large donors — corporations, unions, and wealthy individuals — who used it lose their biggest unregulated route into elections. Incumbent members give up election-year franked mass mailings. Wealthy individuals partly recoup: the individual limit per candidate doubles from $1,000 to $2,000.

drawbacks.text: The bill doubles the individual contribution limit to candidates from $1,000 to $2,000 and indexes it to inflation, which critics of raising limits note favors candidates who can tap networks of larger donors.

Its broad 'express advocacy' definition — covering any paid communication a reasonable person would understand as advocating a candidate's election or defeat within 60 days of an election — would very likely face a First Amendment challenge; the bill itself anticipates this with severability provisions and a fast track for direct Supreme Court review.
It creates new 'State Party Grassroots Funds' with their own $20,000 contribution channels, a carve-out that reform critics could call a new soft-money escape valve for state party activity.
Banning election-year franked mass mailings, personal-use bans, and tighter reporting impose compliance and administrative costs on candidates, small committees, and the FEC.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is shutting down unlimited, unregulated party soft money in exchange for doubling the regulated per-candidate limit and higher disclosure burdens. For voters, the disclosure and soft-money bans are the main win; the doubled limit and the grassroots-fund carve-out are genuine concessions to big donors and parties that soften the reform. The bill is a moderately designed reform, not a sweeping one, and it never came close to being tested.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Rules and Administration Committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote; it sat there until the 105th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Dianne Feinstein introduced the Campaign Reform Act of 1997 on September 18, 1997.
The same day, it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Rules and Administration, and that was its last action in the chamber.
The bill attracted zero cosponsors over its lifetime.
No committee action, hearing-based markup, floor vote, or House counterpart action appears anywhere in the record before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: National party committees and the big soft-money donors who give through them are better off, since the unlimited contributions channel was never closed. Incumbent members also keep their election-year franked mass-mailing privilege.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Party committees and big soft-money donors

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks; it received no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Rules and Administration
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction over election law in the Senate
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on September 18, 1997 and never reported it out or held any action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had zero cosponsors, so there is no record of how support or opposition divided by party.

industries.industry: National and state political party committees
industries.note: They lose the unlimited soft-money channel and restrictions on moving money to 501(c) groups, though they gain a new regulated $20,000-per-donor grassroots fund and a doubled individual contribution limit as partial offsets. Party committees were the principal financial gatekeepers this bill targeted.

industries.industry: Large donors and special interests that fund soft money (corporations, unions, wealthy individuals)
industries.note: They lose the biggest unregulated route for influencing federal elections, but the doubling of the per-candidate limit from $1,000 to $2,000 and indexing restores some of that capacity through regulated channels. Their spending above $10,000 would become publicly disclosed within days.

Party committees could no longer solicit or donate funds to them, cutting off a growing unreported money channel. Their own electioneering spending above $10,000 would face new disclosure requirements.
They lose election-year franked mass mailings and the personal use of campaign funds, both incumbent perks. Campaign committees face higher reporting itemization (down to $50) and bigger penalties.
